turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): sorry we're late, doctor. the car park was a complete joke, and then my sister rang about her scan, they think it's breast cancer, same as mum had, and I just couldn't cut her off.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry, that's a horrible phone call to take. come and sit down. what can I do for you today?

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): well, umm, before I get to me, the neighbour said if it's your face you go straight to A&E and not the GP, and the receptionist had written that the dentist is shut all week, so we thought...
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): just tell him about the tooth, love.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): right, yes, sorry. my cheek's come up and the tooth is throbbing. that's why I'm here.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): ok. which side, and how long has it been like that?

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): the right one, the upper back tooth, where they put the crown on. err, it started two days... no, three days ago. I was fine the evening they fitted it, and the next night it began to throb, and the cheek came up with it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she was up half the night with it, pacing about.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): yes I was in the kitchen with a cold flannel, then a warm one, neither did much, and I kept telling him it isn't sinus because I've had sinus and this is different. it's in the tooth itself, a deep throb, and the gum feels fat.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): any fever with it, or are you just hot from worrying?
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she felt warm to me this morning, I said so.

[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): umm I did take my temperature at home, thirty-seven point something, not dramatic. a mild fever I'd say, and a bit achy, though I can still talk for England as you've noticed.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): and right now, any trouble swallowing, or with your breathing?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): no. swallowing's fine, I managed toast, and my breathing's normal. I got a bit puffed walking up from the car park but that's the hill, not the tooth.

[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. let me look. the right cheek is definitely swollen, tender when I press here, the gum round that crown is red and a bit boggy, but I can't feel a pocket of pus, and you can open your mouth fully.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): it hurts when you press, yes, and when I bite, even soft bread. hot tea sets the throb off, and paracetamol takes the edge off for an hour or two.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): are you taking the paracetamol properly? any other medicines, and any allergies, penicillin in particular?

[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): paracetamol, the five hundred milligram tablets, two of them so a gram. I nearly said two hundred and fifty then, that was years ago, the little ones. the box says up to four times a day, but yesterday I think I only managed three, I forgot lunch, so I'm not sure I'm doing it right. no other medicines. no allergies, penicillin's been fine.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): you had some for your chest last winter, didn't you, and you finished the lot.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): oh yes, amoxicillin, a week, all done, no rash or anything. that was last winter, not now.

[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): ok, nothing current except the paracetamol, and no known allergies. let me see what the nurse wrote. blood pressure one oh nine over seventy-seven, pulse seventy-six, temperature thirty-seven point eight. your last pressure was one-forty over eighty-eight, back in March. weight sixty-eight... no, fifty-eight kilos, she's crossed the six out.

[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): fifty-eight, yes, I've been trying, not that it matters today. uh the tooth though, the dentist filed the crown and said come back if it bit funny, but they're on holiday, nobody answering. I rang four times, left messages, even tried the emergency dental number and it just rang out.

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): mm. so, thinking it through, the crown sits over a tooth that can die off quietly, bacteria get in at the root, and I'm thinking this is an infection under that crowned tooth, a dental abscess starting. the throb, the swollen cheek and that mild temperature all fit, and there's no big collection yet, but these can track if we leave them.

[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): an abscess, right. I was googling at two in the morning, which I know is stupid, and it said Ludwig's something if it goes under the tongue. I checked my tongue and it isn't raised, I don't think.

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): let's not jump to Ludwig's. what I want is an antibiotic now, and a dentist as soon as someone is back. I'm going to prescribe amoxacillin, two hundred and fifty... no, five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for five days, by mouth.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): is that the same one she had last winter?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): yes, same drug, and she tolerated it. take it with food if it upsets your stomach. finish the five days even if the tooth settles.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): three times a day, with food, five days, yes. what if, umm, the swelling...

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): if you get difficulty swallowing, or any trouble breathing, or the swelling jumps, or you feel really unwell, you don't wait for me or the dentist. you go to A&E. that's the bit I need you to hear.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. A&E if I can't swallow or breathe, I've got that. and the pain, do I just carry on with the paracetamol?

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): yes, stick with the gram up to four times a day, and try not to miss doses, it works better regular. ibuprofen as well if your stomach's alright, four hundred milligrams three times a day with food, but only if you want it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): stomach's fine, I might add it. umm, will you want me back, or is it just the dentist?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you here in three days to check the swelling's going down, whether or not the dentist has rung. reception can book it on your way out.
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): three days, I'll make sure she comes. she was going to wait the weekend.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I wasn't going to wait the weekend, I came today, didn't I. anyway if the cheek gets bigger tonight I'm not sitting on it, I'll go up to the hospital like you said.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): good. so amoxacillin five hundred three times a day for five days, paracetamol regular, back here in three days, and A&E if swallowing or breathing becomes difficult. anything else before you go?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): no, I think that's the lot, thank you. sorry again about being late, and there's nothing you can say about my sister really. we'll ring the dentist again in the morning.

spec.situation: Cheek swelling and throbbing toothache for three days after a crown; fever mild; dentist unavailable; doctor prescribes antibiotic, warns about swallowing or breathing difficulty.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Amoxicillin for a week is supported, but chest infection indication is only 'for your chest,' not explicitly infection.
bad.text: amoxicillin (duration=a week, indication=chest infection, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Doctor says no pocket of pus, but body site 'right cheek' is not stated.

omissions.text: No current regular medicines other than paracetamol.
Penicillin specifically has been tolerated before: amoxicillin last winter for a chest infection, finished the full week, with no rash or other reaction.
Home temperature was only 'thirty-seven point something', described by the patient as not dramatic.
Pain described as a deep throb in the tooth itself, different from prior sinus pain.
Able to eat/swallow toast despite the problem.
Pain also triggered by pressure on examination and when biting even soft bread.
Doctor noted there was no big collection yet / no palpable pocket of pus around the area; the recorded exam localises absent pus to the right cheek, which is inaccurate.
Patient had tried a cold flannel and then a warm one, with little benefit.
Crown had recently been filed by the dentist, who advised return if the bite felt wrong.
Dental access issue: dentist on holiday/not answering; patient rang four times, left messages, and the emergency dental number also rang out.
Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food was advised only if the patient wanted it and if her stomach was alright.
Reception was to book the GP review on the way out.
